en: The Bodhicittotpāda-śāstra, Volume One.
Composed by the Bodhisattva Maitreya;
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of Kucha during the Later Qin dynasty.
I pay homage to the Buddhas of the past, future, and present, who are boundless,
whose wisdom is equal to space and immovable, and who are the World-Saviors, the Honored Ones of Great Compassion.
There is the Mahāvaipulya Supreme Sublime Dharma Mātṛkā-piṭaka, which is the practice of the Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas.

That is to say: they encourage and delight others in the cultivation and accumulation of unsurpassed bodhi; they enable sentient beings to give rise to profound and expansive resolve, establishing vows that are definitively adorned; they sacrifice body, life, and wealth to subdue greed and stinginess; they cultivate the five aggregates of precepts to transform and guide those who violate prohibitions; they practice ultimate patience to tame anger and obstruction; they rouse courageous diligence to settle sentient beings in peace; they collect various meditative concentrations to know the minds of the multitude; they practice wisdom to eliminate ignorance; they enter the gate of reality to depart from all attachments; they proclaim and demonstrate the profound practices of emptiness and signlessness; and they extol merits so that the lineage of the Buddhas shall never be severed.

There are such immeasurable skillful means and gates of purification for the dharmas that assist awakening; these should be analyzed and revealed for all those with the highest and most excellent aspirations, so that they may all ultimately attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
O Sons of the Buddha!

If a Son of the Buddha upholds the words of the Buddha and is able to expound the Dharma for the sake of sentient beings, they should first extol the merits of the Buddha. Having heard this, sentient beings will then be able to resolve their minds to seek the wisdom of the Buddha; because they have resolved their minds, the lineage of the Buddhas shall not be severed.

If bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, or upāsikās mindfully recollect the Buddha and the Dharma, they should further recollect that when the Tathāgata was practicing the bodhisattva path, he underwent all manner of diligent hardships for the sake of seeking the Dharma throughout incalculable eons (asaṃkhyeya-kalpa).

With such a thought, if one preaches even a single verse of Dharma to a bodhisattva, and that bodhisattva hears this Dharma and is thereby instructed, exhorted, benefited, and gladdened, they shall plant roots of goodness, cultivate the Buddha-dharma, and attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

In order to sever the various sufferings and afflictions of immeasurable sentient beings throughout beginningless birth and death, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva desires to perfect immeasurable body and mind; they diligently cultivate vigor, deeply resolve great vows, practice great skillful means, give rise to great compassion, and seek great wisdom and the mark of the invisible crown of the head—seeking such great dharmas of all Buddhas as these.
You should know that these dharmas are immeasurable and boundless; because the dharmas are immeasurable, the karmic fruit and reward of merit are likewise immeasurable.

As the Tathāgata has said: "The karmic fruit and reward of merit from even a single inferior thought of initial resolve by a bodhisattva cannot be fully described even in hundreds of thousands of millions of kalpas, let alone the karmic fruit and reward of the various thoughts cultivated over one day, one month, one year, or even a hundred years—how could they ever be fully described?"

Why is this? Because the conduct of a bodhisattva is inexhaustible; it is because they desire to cause all sentient beings to abide in the patience of the non-arising of phenomena (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti) and to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
O Sons of the Buddha!

When a bodhisattva first gives rise to the mind of enlightenment (*bodhicitta*), it is like the initial gradual rising of the great ocean; you should know that it serves as the dwelling place for wish-fulfilling jewels of low, middling, and superior value, up to those of priceless value, for all such jewels are born from the great ocean.

The Bodhisattva’s generation of the mind is also like this: when it first gradually arises, one should know that it becomes the source from which all wholesome dharmas—those of humans, devas, śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, including meditative concentration and wisdom—are produced.

Furthermore, it is like when the trichiliocosm first begins to arise; one should know that it serves as a support and a place of refuge for all sentient beings within the twenty-five realms of existence.

It is the same with the Bodhisattva’s generation of the bodhicitta: when it first gradually arises, it universally acts as a support and a place of refuge for all immeasurable sentient beings—namely those of the six destinies and four modes of birth; those with right view and wrong view; those who cultivate goodness and those who practice evil; those who uphold the pure precepts and those who violate the four grave prohibitions; those who honor the Triple Gem and those who slander the True Dharma; all Māras and non-Buddhists, śramaṇas and brahmins, kṣatriyas, brāhmaṇas, vaiśyas, and śūdras. All these beings are borne by it and take it as their reliance.

Furthermore, when a bodhisattva generates the mind of awakening, compassion is foremost; since a bodhisattva’s compassion is boundless and immeasurable, the generation of this mind has no limit, being equal to the realm of sentient beings.
Just as space universally covers all without exception, so too is the bodhisattva’s production of the mind of enlightenment: there are no sentient beings whom it does not cover.
Just as the realm of sentient beings is immeasurable, boundless, and inexhaustible, so too is the bodhisattva’s production of the mind of enlightenment: immeasurable, boundless, and without end.

Because space is inexhaustible, sentient beings are inexhaustible; because sentient beings are inexhaustible, the bodhisattva’s resolve for awakening is equal to the realm of sentient beings, and the realm of sentient beings has no limit.
I shall now, following the holy intent, explain a small portion of it.

Taking all the Buddha-worlds in the eastern direction—numbering as many as the sands of a thousand billion *asaṃkhyeya* Ganges Rivers—and likewise in the south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, and above and below, each numbering as many as the sands of a thousand billion *asaṃkhyeya* Ganges Rivers, and grinding them all down into dust: these minute particles would not even come into contact with the physical eye.

If all sentient beings in as many trichiliocosm great thousandfold world systems as there are in hundreds of billions of *asaṃkhyeya* Ganges-sands were to gather together and take up one particle of dust; and if sentient beings in two hundred billion *asaṃkhyeya* Ganges-sands of trichiliocosm great thousandfold world systems were to take up two particles of dust; and if this process were continued until all the earth-element particles in thousands of billions of Buddha-worlds in each of the ten directions—as many as hundreds of billions of *asaṃkhyeya* Ganges-sands—were completely exhausted, the realm of sentient beings would still not be exhausted.

It is, for example, like a person who splits a single hair into one hundred parts and uses one part of that hair to take up a drop of water from the great ocean; the small portion of sentient beings I have now described is just like this, while those not so described are like the waters of the great ocean. Even if all Buddhas were to expound extensive parables for immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, they would still not reach the end of it.
The Bodhisattva’s resolve is able to completely encompass all such sentient beings.
How is this so, O Sons of the Buddha?
Can this bodhicitta ever be exhausted?

If there is a bodhisattva who, upon hearing such a teaching, is not startled, not terrified, does not retreat, and does not sink in despair, one should know that this person is certainly able to give rise to the mind of enlightenment (*bodhicitta*); even if all the infinite Buddhas were to praise their merits for immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, they could never be exhausted.
Why is this? Because this bodhicitta is without limit and inexhaustible, it possesses such immeasurable benefits as these.
Therefore, it is proclaimed so that sentient beings may universally receive and practice it, and thus give rise to the bodhicitta.
Chapter Two: On Generating the Resolve The *Bodhicittotpādana-śāstra*: Chapter Two, On Generating the Resolve. How does a bodhisattva generate the resolve for enlightenment (*bodhicitta*)?
By what causes and conditions does one cultivate and accumulate enlightenment?

If a bodhisattva draws near to spiritual friends, makes offerings to the Buddhas, cultivates and accumulates roots of goodness, aspires to seek the supreme Dharma, maintains a mind that is always gentle and pliant, is able to endure suffering when it encounters hardship, possesses profound and thick compassion, maintains a deep-seated equanimity, has faith and delight in the Mahāyāna, and seeks the wisdom of a Buddha.
If a person can possess these ten dharmas, they are then able to resolve their mind upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Furthermore, there are four conditions for resolving the mind to cultivate and accumulate unsurpassed enlightenment.
What are these four?

First, generating the bodhicitta by reflecting upon all Buddhas; second, generating the bodhicitta by contemplating the faults and afflictions of the body; third, generating the bodhicitta out of compassion for sentient beings; and fourth, generating the bodhicitta in pursuit of the most supreme fruit.

There are five further matters for contemplating the Buddhas: first, contemplating how the Buddhas of the past, future, and present in the ten directions initially resolved their minds to attain enlightenment; though they possessed the nature of afflictions just as I do now, they ultimately achieved perfect awakening and became Unsurpassed Honored Ones.
For this reason, one generates the bodhicitta.
Second, one reflects that all Buddhas of the three periods of time have each displayed great courage and were able to attain unsurpassed bodhi;
if this bodhi is a dharma that can be attained, then I too should attain it.
For this reason, one generates the bodhicitta.

Third, one contemplates how all Buddhas of the three periods of time generated great wisdom; within the shell of ignorance, they established the supreme mind and accumulated ascetic practices, thereby being able to extricate themselves and transcend the triple world.
I, too, shall do likewise, and must extricate and deliver myself.
For this reason, one generates the bodhicitta.
Fourth, one reflects that all Buddhas of the three periods of time are heroes among men, who have all crossed over the great ocean of birth-and-death and afflictions;
I too am a man, and I shall likewise be able to cross over.
For this reason, one resolves upon bodhicitta.
Fifth, one contemplates that all Buddhas of the three periods of time have aroused great diligence, sacrificing their bodies, lives, and wealth to seek omniscience;
I too shall now follow and train as those Buddhas did.
One generates the bodhicitta for the sake of these matters.

Furthermore, there are five ways in which one observes the faults and afflictions of the body to generate the bodhicitta: first, by observing that one’s own body—comprising the five aggregates and the four great elements—is capable of producing immeasurable evil karma, and thus desires to abandon it.
Second, one contemplates one's own body as constantly discharging foul, impure substances from its nine orifices, thereby giving rise to weary detachment.
Third, one contemplates that one's own body possesses the immeasurable afflictions of greed, hatred, and delusion which incinerate the wholesome mind, desiring to eliminate them.
Fourth, one observes one’s own body as being like a bubble or foam, arising and perishing from moment to moment; because it is a phenomenon that must be abandoned, one desires to cast it aside.

Fifth, one observes that one’s own body is shrouded by ignorance and constantly creates evil karma, wandering through the six realms of existence without benefit; therefore, one seeks the most supreme fruit and resolves to attain bodhicitta.

Furthermore, there are five matters: first, seeing all Tathāgatas adorned with the marks and signs of excellence, their radiance pure and penetrating, which removes affliction for those who encounter them, for the purpose of cultivating and accumulating [these qualities].
Second, it is because one perceives that the *dharmakāya* of all Tathāgatas is eternally abiding, pure, and undefiled, in order to cultivate and accumulate [this realization].

Third, it is because one perceives that all Tathāgatas possess the pure collection of dharmas consisting of ethical discipline (*śīla*), meditative concentration (*samādhi*), wisdom (*prajñā*), liberation (*vimukti*), and the knowledge and vision of liberation (*vimuktijñānadarśana*), in order to cultivate and accumulate [this realization].
Fourth, seeing that all Tathāgatas possess the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, great compassion, and the three foundations of mindfulness, for the sake of cultivating and accumulating them.
Fifth, seeing that all Tathāgatas possess omniscience, whose compassionate pity universally covers all sentient beings, and who are able to lead all the ignorant and deluded onto the right path.
For the sake of cultivation and accumulation, one generates the bodhicitta out of compassion for sentient beings.

Furthermore, there are five matters: first, seeing that sentient beings are bound by ignorance; second, seeing that sentient beings are entangled in manifold sufferings; third, seeing that sentient beings accumulate unwholesome karma; fourth, seeing that sentient beings commit extremely grave evils; and fifth, seeing that sentient beings do not cultivate the True Dharma.

There are four further matters bound by ignorance: first, seeing all sentient beings deluded by folly and craving as they undergo great and intense suffering; second, seeing all sentient beings who do not believe in cause and effect and thus commit evil deeds; third, seeing all sentient beings who abandon the True Dharma and instead believe in and accept false paths; and fourth, seeing all sentient beings submerged in the river of afflictions, drifting along with the four currents.

There are four further matters concerning those entangled by manifold sufferings: first, seeing that sentient beings fear birth, old age, sickness, and death, yet do not seek liberation and instead continue to create karma;
second, seeing that sentient beings constantly engage in activities amidst grief, lamentation, affliction, and suffering without ever resting;
third, seeing that sentient beings experience the suffering of separation from loved ones, yet fail to awaken and instead employ skillful means to become defiled by attachment.
Fourth, seeing that sentient beings constantly give rise to resentment and jealousy due to the suffering of encountering those they hate, and further create enmity.

There are four matters by which one accumulates unwholesome karma: first, seeing sentient beings commit various evils for the sake of craving and desire; second, seeing sentient beings who know that desire gives rise to suffering yet do not abandon it; third, seeing sentient beings who, though seeking happiness, do not fulfill the feet of the precepts; fourth, seeing sentient beings who, though not delighting in suffering, do not cease creating it.
There are four further matters by which one creates extremely grave evil: first, seeing sentient beings violate the heavy precepts, yet remaining heedless despite their anxiety and fear;
second, seeing sentient beings commit the five heinous acts of immediate retribution, yet being so stubborn and perverse as to conceal themselves and feel no shame or remorse;
third, seeing sentient beings slander and destroy the Mahāyāna Vaipulya True Dharma, yet persisting in foolish self-attachment and giving rise to arrogance.
Fourth, seeing that sentient beings, though possessing intelligence and wisdom, have severed their roots of goodness, yet instead become arrogant and never repent or reform.

There are four further matters regarding the failure to cultivate the True Dharma: first, seeing sentient beings born into the eight difficult circumstances, where they do not hear the True Dharma and do not know how to practice goodness;
second, seeing sentient beings encounter a Buddha’s appearance in the world, yet being unable to receive and uphold the preaching of the True Dharma.
Third, seeing sentient beings who, having become attached to external paths, afflict their bodies and cultivate practices that are eternally devoid of the essential means for liberation;

fourth, seeing sentient beings who, having cultivated and attained the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, claim it to be nirvana, only to fall back into the three miserable realms once their wholesome retribution is exhausted.

Seeing that sentient beings create karma through ignorance and suffer for a long night, abandoning the True Dharma and being deluded regarding the path out, the Bodhisattva gives rise to great compassion for their sake and resolves to seek Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi as if his head were on fire.
For all sentient beings who possess suffering and affliction, I shall rescue and deliver them so that none remain.
O Sons of the Buddha!
I have now briefly explained the arousal of the mind through the causal conditions for a bodhisattva’s initial practice; were it to be explained in detail, it would be immeasurable and boundless.
Chapter Three: On Vows and Aspirations. In the *Bodhicittotpāda-śāstra*, Chapter Three: How does a bodhisattva set out toward enlightenment?
By what karmic practices does one accomplish enlightenment?
When a Bodhisattva who has resolved their mind dwells on the Stage of Dry Wisdom, they should first firmly establish right vows to gather in all immeasurable sentient beings:
"I seek unsurpassed Bodhi in order to rescue, protect, deliver, and liberate them all without exception, leading them all ultimately to Nirvana without remainder."

Therefore, at the initial moment of generating the mind of enlightenment, great compassion is foremost; by means of this compassionate mind, one is able to give rise to ten successive and increasingly superior right vows.
What are these ten?

May the roots of goodness planted by me in previous lives as well as in this present body be bestowed upon all infinite sentient beings; may they together dedicate these roots of goodness toward unsurpassed enlightenment.
May this vow of mine increase with every thought-moment; may it always remain bound to my heart in every life I am born into, never to be forgotten, and may it be protected by dhāraṇīs.

May I, having dedicated this toward great enlightenment, through these roots of goodness, always be able to make offerings to all Buddhas in every place of birth, and may I never be born in a land where no Buddha resides.

May I, having been born in the lands of all Buddhas, always be able to draw near to and attend upon them at their side, like a shadow following a form, never being separated from the Buddhas for even a single moment.
"May I, having attained proximity to the Buddha, receive from him the teaching appropriate for me, whereby I may immediately achieve the five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*) of a bodhisattva.

May I, having achieved the five supernormal powers of a bodhisattva, be able to penetrate the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) as it is disseminated through provisional names, understand the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) as its true nature, and attain the wisdom of the True Dharma."

May I, having attained the wisdom of the True Dharma, preach it for the sake of sentient beings with an insatiable mind, instructing, exhorting, benefiting, and gladdening them so that all may attain understanding.

May I, having brought all sentient beings to understanding, travel by the spiritual power of the Buddha to all worlds throughout the ten directions without exception, making offerings to all Buddhas, hearing and receiving the True Dharma, and extensively gathering in sentient beings.

May I, having received the true Dharma from all Buddhas, be able to immediately turn the pure wheel of Dharma; and may all sentient beings in the worlds of the ten directions who hear my Dharma or hear my name immediately abandon all afflictions and give rise to the bodhicitta.

May I cause all sentient beings to resolve upon bodhicitta, and having done so, may I constantly follow and protect them, removing what is unbeneficial and bestowing immeasurable happiness; may I sacrifice my body, life, and wealth to gather in sentient beings and shoulder the burden of the True Dharma.

May I, having taken up the burden of the True Dharma, practice the True Dharma with a mind that has nothing to practice—just as the various Bodhisattvas practice the True Dharma, neither practicing nor not practicing.
To transform sentient beings without abandoning one's right vows—this is called the ten great right vows of the bodhisattva who has resolved to attain enlightenment.
These ten great vows pervade the realm of sentient beings and encompass all vows as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
If all sentient beings were to be exhausted, my vow would then be exhausted; yet since sentient beings are truly inexhaustible, this great vow of mine is likewise without end.
Furthermore, giving is the cause of bodhi, for it gathers in and sustains all sentient beings.
Observing the precepts is the cause of bodhi, for it fulfills all virtues and completes one's original vows.
Patience is the cause of bodhi, for it brings to fruition the thirty-two marks and eighty secondary characteristics.
Diligence is the cause of bodhi, for it increases virtuous conduct and zealously teaches all sentient beings.
Meditative concentration is the cause of bodhi, for the bodhisattva skillfully disciplines himself and is able to know the various mental activities of sentient beings.
Wisdom is the cause of bodhi, for it is fully capable of knowing the nature and characteristics of all phenomena.

To state the essential point: the six pāramitās are the direct cause of bodhi, while the four immeasurable minds, the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, and all myriad virtuous practices collectively assist in its accomplishment.
If a bodhisattva cultivates and accumulates the six pāramitās, according to their practice, they will gradually draw near to anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
O Sons of the Buddha!
Those who seek awakening should not be negligent, for negligent conduct can destroy the roots of goodness.
If a bodhisattva subdues the six sense faculties and remains vigilant, such a person is able to cultivate the six pāramitās.

When a bodhisattva first gives rise to the aspiration for enlightenment, they first establish sincerity and make a resolute vow. One who has made such a vow never again succumbs to negligence, indolence, or laxity. Why is this?
One establishes a firm vow because it is sustained by five matters:

first, being able to make the mind steadfast; second, being able to subdue the afflictions (*kleśa*); third, being able to ward off negligence; fourth, being able to destroy the five hindrances (*pañca-nīvaraṇa*); and fifth, being able to diligently practice the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*).
As the Buddha praised: "The Tathāgata,
the Honored One of Great Wisdom, has clearly explained the realization of merit,
the power of patience, wisdom, and meritorious deeds, and the supreme power of his vow."
"What is meant by making a vow?
It is that if someone comes and seeks various things from me, I shall at that time give whatever I have, never giving rise to even a single thought of stinginess."

If, for even the duration of a finger-snap, I should give rise to an evil thought while seeking a pure reward through the causes and conditions of giving, I would then be deceiving the immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable Buddhas currently residing throughout the worlds of the ten directions; furthermore, in future ages, I shall certainly not attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
If I uphold the precepts, even at the cost of my life, I shall establish a pure mind and vow never to waver or regret.
If I cultivate patience, even when harmed or even maimed by others, I shall constantly give rise to loving-kindness and vow never to harbor anger or resentment.

If I practice diligence, even when encountering cold or heat, kings or bandits, water or fire, lions, tigers, or wolves, or places devoid of water and grain, I shall resolutely strengthen my mind and vow never to retreat or sink in spirit.

If I practice dhyāna, I shall not allow my mind to be distracted by external matters; I must bind my mindfulness to the object of meditation, vowing never to give rise for even a moment to unlawful or chaotic thoughts.

If I cultivate and accumulate wisdom, observing the true nature of all phenomena as they are, and accordingly upholding them, I shall not give rise to dualistic views regarding what is wholesome or unwholesome, conditioned or unconditioned, or saṃsāra or nirvāṇa.

If my mind gives rise to regret, anger, hindrance, despondency, or distracted thoughts, or if I give rise to two views for even as long as a finger-snap, yet seek a pure reward through precepts, patience, diligence, meditation, and wisdom, I would then be deceiving the immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable Buddhas currently residing throughout the worlds of the ten directions; furthermore, in future ages, I shall certainly not attain Anuttara-samyak-sambodhi.

By means of the ten great vows, the Bodhisattva upholds the practice of the True Dharma; by means of the six great oaths, he restrains the mind from negligence. Thus, he will certainly be able to diligently cultivate and accumulate the six pāramitās, attaining Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Chapter Four: The Perfection of Giving (*Dānapāramitā*) from the *Bodhicittotpāda-śāstra*. How does a bodhisattva practice giving?
If giving is performed for the benefit of oneself, the benefit of others, or the benefit of both, such giving can adorn the path to enlightenment.
The Bodhisattva practices giving because he desires to discipline sentient beings and cause them to be free from suffering and affliction.

One who cultivates the practice of giving constantly gives rise to a mind of renunciation toward their own wealth and possessions, and conceives a mind of reverence toward those who come to seek it, regarding them as parents, teachers, elders, and spiritual friends.
To give rise to a heart of compassion toward those who are poor and lowly, regarding them as one's only child, and to provide whatever they require with a joyful mind and respectful reverence—
this is called the Bodhisattva’s initial cultivation of the mind of giving.
By practicing generosity, one’s good reputation spreads far and wide, and in whatever place one is born, wealth and treasures are abundant; this is called self-benefit.
Being able to satisfy the minds of sentient beings, teaching and taming them so that they are free from stinginess, is called benefiting others.
By means of the great gift of signlessness cultivated by oneself, one transforms all sentient beings so that they share in one's own benefit; this is called mutual benefit (*ubhayārtha*).

Through the cultivation of giving, one attains the status of a Wheel-Turning King (*cakravartin*), gathering in all immeasurable sentient beings, and eventually attains the Buddha’s inexhaustible treasury of Dharma; this is called adorning the path to enlightenment (*bodhimārga*).
There are three kinds of giving: first, the gift of the Dharma; second, the gift of fearlessness; and third, the gift of material wealth.

As for the gift of the Dharma, it consists of encouraging others to receive the precepts and cultivate the mind of renunciation; explaining the faults and calamities of the four inversions—namely, the views of nihilism and eternalism—in order to destroy false views; analyzing and revealing the meaning of the ultimate truth; praising the merit of diligence; and speaking of the evils of negligence. This is called the gift of the Dharma.

If there are sentient beings who fear kings, lions, tigers, wolves, water, fire, or bandits, and the Bodhisattva, having seen them, is able to provide protection and rescue, this is called the gift of fearlessness.

To give away one's own wealth and possessions without stinginess—ranging from the highest treasures such as elephants, horses, chariots, silks, grains, clothing, and food, down to a handful of flour or a single thread—giving according to the needs of the seeker and in accordance with their wishes, whether much or little, is called the gift of material wealth (*āmiṣadāna*).

Furthermore, there are five kinds of material giving (*āmiṣadāna*): first, giving with a sincere mind; second, giving with a faithful mind; third, giving at the appropriate time; fourth, giving with one's own hands; and fifth, giving in accordance with the Dharma.
There are furthermore five things that should not be given as gifts: giving wealth acquired through unrighteous means to others, because the object is impure;
and giving alcohol or poisonous drugs to others, because they cause confusion among sentient beings.
One does not bestow snares, nets, or traps upon others, for they afflict sentient beings.
One does not bestow swords, staves, bows, or arrows upon others, for they harm sentient beings.
One does not bestow music or female beauty upon others, for they destroy the pure mind.
To state the essential point: anything that is not in accordance with the Dharma and which disturbs or harms sentient beings should not be given to others.
All other things that can bring peace and happiness to sentient beings are called "Dharma-conforming gifts" (*dharmānukūla-dāna*).

Those who delight in giving further obtain five kinds of renown and virtuous benefits: first, they constantly gain proximity to all worthy sages and saints; second, they are joyfully beheld by all sentient beings; third, when entering a great assembly, they are honored and respected by others; fourth, their good name and excellent reputation spread throughout the ten directions; and fifth, they are able to serve as a supreme and wondrous cause for awakening.
A bodhisattva is called "one who gives all" (sarvadāyaka); being one who gives all does not mean possessing great wealth, but refers to the mind of giving.
Seeking wealth in accordance with the Dharma and maintaining it for the purpose of giving is what is called "giving all."
Giving with a pure mind free from flattery and crookedness is called "giving everything.
Giving with a heart of compassion upon seeing those who are poor is called "giving everything.
Giving with a heart of loving-kindness and compassion upon seeing those in distress and suffering is called "giving everything."
To practice giving despite living in poverty with few resources is called "universal giving.
To give away cherished and precious possessions with an open mind is called "universal giving.
To give without discriminating between fields of merit—whether they observe the precepts or violate them, or whether they are worthy recipients or not—is called "universal giving."
Giving without seeking the sublime and virtuous pleasures of humans or devas is called the giving of all.
Giving with the resolve to seek unexcelled great bodhi is called the giving of all.
Giving without regret before, during, or after the act of giving is called the giving of all.
If one gives flowers as an offering, it is because they are endowed with the flowers of the *dhāraṇīs* and the seven factors of awakening (*saptabodhyaṅga*).
If one gives incense as an offering, it is because they are endowed with the perfuming and anointing of the body through morality, concentration, and wisdom.
If one gives fruit as an offering, it is because they have fully accomplished the fruition that is free from outflows (*anāsrava-phala*).
If one gives food as a gift, it is because it fulfills life, eloquence, physical beauty, strength, and happiness.
If one gives clothing as a gift, it is because it fulfills pure physical appearance and removes shamelessness and lack of decorum.
By giving lamps as an offering, one fulfills the Buddha-eye, for it illuminates the nature of all dharmas.
By giving elephants, horses, and carriages, one attains the Unsurpassed Vehicle (Anuttarayāna), for it is endowed with supernormal powers (abhijñā).
By giving necklaces as a gift, one fulfills the eighty minor marks (anuvyañjana).
By giving precious jewels as a gift, one fulfills the thirty-two marks of a great man (mahāpuruṣa-lakṣaṇa).
By giving servants and laborers endowed with physical strength as a gift, one fulfills the ten powers (bala) and four fearlessnesses (vaiśāradya) of a Buddha.

To speak briefly, even up to his kingdom, city, wife, children, head, eyes, hands, and feet—he gives his entire body with a heart free from stinginess, for the sake of attaining unsurpassed bodhi and delivering all sentient beings.
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices generosity, they do not perceive the material objects, the giver, or the recipient.
Because it is signless, this constitutes the fulfillment of the dāna-pāramitā.
Chapter Five: The Perfection of Śīla. In the *Bodhicittotpāda-śāstra*, Chapter Five, "The Perfection of Śīla," it is asked: How does a bodhisattva practice and maintain ethical discipline (*śīla*)?
If one maintains the precepts for the sake of one's own benefit, the benefit of others, or the benefit of both, such observance of the precepts can adorn the path to enlightenment.
A bodhisattva maintains the precepts because they desire to discipline sentient beings and cause them to be free from suffering and affliction.

One who cultivates the precepts completely purifies all actions of body, speech, and mind; they are able to abandon and distance themselves from unwholesome conduct; they are skilled at censuring evil deeds and the violation of prohibitions; and their minds are constantly filled with dread regarding even minor transgressions—this is called the Bodhisattva’s initial resolve for upholding the precepts.
By practicing and upholding the precepts, one remains far removed from all evil faults and afflictions and is always reborn in auspicious realms; this is called self-benefit.
To transform and guide sentient beings so that they do not commit evil is called benefiting others.
To direct one’s own cultivation toward the precepts of enlightenment and transform all sentient beings so that they likewise attain their own benefit is called "mutual benefit.

By virtue of practicing and maintaining the precepts, one attains freedom from desire, up to the exhaustion of outflows and the realization of supreme perfect enlightenment; this is called "adorning the path to enlightenment."
There are three kinds of precepts: first, those of the body; second, those of speech; and third, those of the mind. Regarding the observance of bodily precepts:

one must forever abandon all acts of killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct; one must not deprive living beings of their lives, encroach upon the property of others, or violate the purity of another’s person; furthermore, one must not create the causes or the means for killing and the like, nor harm sentient beings with sticks, wood, tiles, or stones.
If an object belongs to another or is being used by another, one does not take even a single blade of grass or a single leaf without it being given.
Furthermore, one never casts a lewd glance at subtle forms; in all four modes of deportment, one is respectful, prudent, and circumspect. This is called the precept of the body.

One who maintains the precept of speech abandons all false speech, divisive speech, harsh speech, and frivolous speech; they never deceive or cause estrangement between those in harmony, nor do they slander, revile, or use flowery rhetoric, nor do they employ skillful means to annoy or provoke others.

To speak with utmost sincerity, gentleness, loyalty, and trustworthiness; to always speak for the benefit of others, exhorting and transforming them to cultivate goodness—this is called the precept of speech.

As for upholding the precept of mind: it consists in eliminating greed, anger, and false views; constantly cultivating a gentle heart; refraining from committing transgressions; believing that such karmic offenses result in evil retributions; not creating any evils through the power of contemplation; regarding even minor offenses as extremely grave; and feeling fear, anxiety, and regret should one commit them even by mistake.

Not giving rise to anger or vexation toward sentient beings; having seen sentient beings, giving rise to a heart of affectionate regard; knowing kindness and repaying it with a heart free from stinginess; delighting in performing meritorious deeds and constantly transforming others through them; and constantly cultivating a mind of loving-kindness to have compassion for all—this is called the precept of the mind.

These precepts of the ten wholesome actions bring five benefits: first, they can restrain unwholesome conduct; second, they can give rise to a virtuous mind; third, they can obstruct the afflictions; fourth, they accomplish a pure mind; and fifth, they can increase one's ethical discipline.

If a person skillfully cultivates the practice of heedfulness and is endowed with right mindfulness to discern good and evil, it should be known that this person is certainly able to cultivate the precepts of the ten wholesome courses of action.
The eighty-four thousand immeasurable categories of precepts are all subsumed within the ten wholesome precepts.

These ten wholesome precepts can serve as the foundation for all wholesome precepts; by severing the evils of body, speech, and mind, they are able to restrain all unwholesome dharmas, and are therefore called "precepts" (śīla).

There are five kinds of precepts: first, the prātimokṣa precept; second, the precept concomitant with meditative concentration (dhyāna-samvara); third, the untainted precept (anāsrava-śīla); fourth, the precept of guarding the sense faculties; and fifth, the unmanifest precept (avijñapti-śīla).
The Prātimokṣa precepts are received from a teacher through the ritual of one motion and three proclamations (jñapti-caturtha-karman); this is called the Prātimokṣa vow.
The four fundamental dhyānas and the four preparatory stages (anāgamya-dhyāna) are called the vow concomitant with meditative concentration (samādhi-sahaja-śīla).
The fundamental four dhyānas and the threshold stage of the first dhyāna are called untainted precepts (*anāsrava-śīla*).

Restraining the sense faculties and cultivating right mindfulness so that seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting, and touching forms, sounds, odors, flavors, and tangibles do not give rise to negligence is called the precept of restraining the faculties (*indriya-saṃvara-śīla*).
To refrain from committing further evil after leaving this body and entering the next life is called the precept of non-action (*avijñapti-śīla*).

When a bodhisattva cultivates the precepts, they do not share them with śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas; because they are not shared, they are called "well-maintained precepts. Because they are well-maintained, they are able to benefit all sentient beings.
One maintains the precept of loving-kindness (*maitrī*) in order to rescue and protect sentient beings, bringing them peace and happiness.
One maintains the precept of compassion (*karuṇā*) in order to endure all sufferings and uproot them from peril and distress.
One maintains the precept of sympathetic joy (*muditā*) in order to delight in the cultivation of goodness without indolence.
One upholds the precept of equanimity because one abandons both attachment and aversion, treating enemies and kin with equality.
One upholds the precept of giving because one teaches, transforms, and subdues all sentient beings.
One upholds the precept of patience because the mind is always supple and free from anger or obstruction.
One upholds the precept of diligence because wholesome karma increases daily without retrogression;
one upholds the precept of meditative concentration because one abandons desire and unwholesomeness while cultivating the factors of dhyāna;
one upholds the precept of wisdom because one never tires of hearing the Dharma and cultivating roots of goodness.
One upholds the precept of associating with virtuous friends in order to assist in the accomplishment of the unsurpassed path to Bodhi;
one upholds the precept of distancing oneself from evil associates in order to abandon the three evil realms and the eight difficult conditions.

When a bodhisattva maintains pure precepts, they do not rely on the desire realm, do not approach the form realm, and do not dwell in the formless realm; this is the pure precept. It is the pure precept that abandons the dust of desire, removes the obstruction of ill-will, and extinguishes the veil of ignorance.
To remain free from the two extremes of annihilationism and eternalism, and not to contradict dependent origination, is the pure precept.
To be unattached to the marks of the conventional designations of form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness is the pure precept.
Not being bound by causes, not giving rise to various views, and not dwelling in doubt or regret—this is pure precept.
Not dwelling in the three unwholesome roots of greed, hatred, and delusion—this is pure precept.
Not dwelling in conceit, arrogance, overweening pride, pride of self, or great pride; being gentle, kind, and compliant—this is the pure precept.
Being unmoved by gain or loss, disrepute or fame, praise or blame, suffering or pleasure—this is the pure precept.
Not being stained by the false and provisional designations of worldly truth, but conforming to ultimate truth, is the pure precept.
Being without affliction or feverish distress, characterized by quiescence and detachment from signs, is the pure precept.

To state the essentials: even to the point of not begrudging one's own body or life, contemplating the perception of impermanence to give rise to weary detachment, and diligently practicing roots of goodness with courageous and vigorous effort—this is pure precept.
When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva practices and maintains the precepts, they do not perceive a pure mind because they are free from conceptualization; this is the fulfillment of the Śīla-pāramitā.
Chapter Six: The Perfection of Patience (*Kṣāntipāramitā*) from the *Bodhicittotpāda-śāstra*. Regarding the sixth chapter on the perfection of patience: how does a bodhisattva practice patience?
If patience is practiced for the sake of one's own benefit, the benefit of others, or the benefit of both, such patience can adorn the path to Bodhi.
A bodhisattva cultivates patience in order to subdue sentient beings and cause them to leave behind suffering and affliction.

One who cultivates patience always maintains a mind of humility toward all sentient beings; they abandon and do not practice harshness or arrogance. Upon seeing those who are coarse or evil, they give rise to a heart of compassion; their speech is always gentle as they exhort and transform others to cultivate goodness. They are able to explain with discernment the differences between the karmic retributions of anger and harmonious patience. This is called the Bodhisattva’s initial mind of patience.
By practicing patience, one distances oneself from all evils and attains peace and happiness of body and mind; this is called self-benefit.
To transform and guide sentient beings so that they all become harmonious and compliant is called benefiting others.
To transform all sentient beings by means of the unsurpassed great patience one has cultivated oneself, causing them to share in one's own benefit, is called "mutual benefit" (*ubhayārtha*).

By practicing patience, one attains an upright and handsome appearance, becoming an object of veneration for others, and ultimately attaining the Buddha’s supreme and wondrous marks and signs; this is called "adorning the path to enlightenment."
There are three kinds of patience: namely, patience of body, speech, and mind.
What is patience of body?
It is when one is able to endure entirely all harms, insults, beatings, and even injuries inflicted by others.
To see all sentient beings in peril and fear, and to take their place with one’s own body without weariness or indolence—this is called patience of the body (*kāyakṣānti*).
What is patience of speech (*vāk-kṣānti*)?
If one sees someone reviling, to receive it silently without retorting; this is patience of speech.
If one encounters those who come to reproach and revile one unreasonably, one should respond with gentle words and compliance;
if others falsely accuse or maliciously slander one, all such things should be endured. This is called patience of speech.
What is patience of the mind?

When seeing one who is angry, the mind harbors no resentment; if there is provocation, the mind remains undisturbed; and if there is slander or defamation, the mind likewise feels no enmity—this is called patience of the mind.
In this world, there are two kinds of beatings: first, those that are justified; second, those that are unjustified.

If one has committed an offense, or if one is struck by another out of suspicion or resentment, one should endure it as if taking ambrosia (amṛta) and should instead cultivate reverence toward that person.
Why is this? Because they are able to skillfully instruct and discipline me, enabling me to leave behind all faults and transgressions.
If someone should maliciously inflict harm upon me, I should reflect to myself:
I am currently without fault; this must be the result summoned by past karmic deeds from previous lives, and thus it should be endured.
Furthermore, one should reflect:
"The four elements are a mere provisional combination, and the five aggregates are a convergence of conditions—who is there to receive these blows?"
Furthermore, one should observe that the person before one is like a fool or a madman; I ought to have compassion for them—how could I not exercise patience?
Moreover, there are two kinds of those who revile: first, those who speak truthfully, and second, those who speak falsely.
If what is said is true, I ought to feel shame;
if it is false, it concerns nothing of my own, being like an echo or like the passing of wind—causing me no harm—and therefore I should endure it with patience.
Furthermore, it is the same with anger: if another comes to me in anger, I should endure it;
for if I were to become angry with them, I would fall into the evil realms in future lives and undergo great suffering and distress.

For this reason, even if my body were to be hacked, severed, and dismembered, I should not give rise to anger; rather, I should deeply contemplate the causal conditions of past karma and cultivate loving-kindness and compassion for all beings.

If I cannot endure such minor suffering, I shall be unable to discipline my own mind; how then could I possibly discipline sentient beings, enabling them to attain liberation from all unwholesome dharmas and achieve the unsurpassed fruit?

If there is a wise person who delights in practicing patience, that person will always possess a handsome countenance and abundant wealth; when others see them, they will rejoice, look up to them with reverence, and submit to their will.

Furthermore, one should observe that if a person has a deformed body, an ugly complexion, impaired faculties, or lacks material wealth, one should know that these are all obtained through the causes and conditions of anger.
For these reasons, the wise should cultivate patience (*kṣānti*) deeply.

There are ten matters that serve as the causes and conditions for the patience toward living beings (*sattvakṣānti*): first, not contemplating the marks of "self" or "what belongs to self"; second, not dwelling on one's lineage; third, destroying arrogance; fourth, not retaliating when evil is encountered; fifth, contemplating the perception of impermanence (*anityasaṃjñā*); sixth, cultivating loving-kindness and compassion (*maitrī-karuṇā*); seventh, keeping the mind from negligence; eighth, relinquishing hunger, thirst, suffering, pleasure, and other such states; ninth, severing anger and resentment; and tenth, practicing wisdom (*prajñā*).
If a person can accomplish these ten matters, one should know that such a person is able to cultivate patience (*kṣānti*).

When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva cultivates pure, ultimate patience, if they enter into emptiness (*śūnyatā*), signlessness (*animitta*), wishlessness (*apraṇihita*), and non-action (*anabhisaṃskāra*), they do not associate with views, cognitions, wishes, or actions; nor do they rely upon or cling to emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, or non-action. Since all these views, cognitions, wishes, and actions are empty, such patience is characterized by non-duality; this is called pure, ultimate patience.

Whether entering the exhaustion of fetters (*āsravakṣaya*) or entering into cessation (*nirvāṇa*), one does not conjoin with fetters or birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*). One does not rely upon the exhaustion of fetters or cessation; all fetters, birth-and-death, and emptiness are empty. Such patience is characterized by non-duality; it is called the pure, ultimate patience (*viśuddha-atyantakṣānti*).

If a nature does not arise from itself, does not arise from another, and does not arise from a combination [of causes], and if it is neither produced nor destructible—being indestructible, it is inexhaustible; such patience is characterized by non-duality, and this is called the pure, ultimate patience.

Non-action is not action; it is without dependence or attachment, without discrimination, without adornment, without cultivation, and without exertion. It ultimately does not produce anything. Such patience as this is the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
When a bodhisattva practices this patience in this way, they attain the patience of receiving the prediction of enlightenment.
Because the nature and characteristics of patience are entirely empty and there is no sentient being, the bodhisattva mahāsattva who practices patience thus fulfills the pāramitā of kṣānti.
