Chapter Seven: The Perfection of Vigor (Vīryapāramitā). What is the bodhisattva’s practice of vigor?
If diligence is for the sake of one's own benefit, the benefit of others, or the benefit of both, such diligence can adorn the path to enlightenment.
A bodhisattva cultivates diligence because they desire to subdue sentient beings and cause them to be free from suffering and affliction.

One who cultivates diligence constantly and assiduously practices and accumulates pure brahmacarya at all times; abandoning indolence and remaining heedful, their mind remains ever diligent even amidst hardships and unbeneficial circumstances, never falling back or becoming discouraged—this is called the bodhisattva’s first resolve of diligence.
By cultivating diligence, one is able to attain the supreme and wondrous wholesome dharmas of both the mundane and supramundane realms; this is called self-benefit.
To teach and transform sentient beings so that they diligently cultivate goodness is called benefiting others.
To transform all sentient beings by means of the very same right causes for awakening that one has cultivated oneself, so that they may share in one’s own benefit, is called "mutual benefit.

By cultivating diligence, one attains ever more superior, pure, and wondrous fruits, transcending all stages (*bhūmi*) until swiftly achieving perfect enlightenment; this is called "adorned with the path to awakening."
There are two kinds of diligence: first, that which is for the sake of seeking the unsurpassed path; second, that which arises from the broad desire to uproot and rescue all suffering.
Only when a bodhisattva accomplishes the ten recollections can they resolve their mind to practice diligence with vigor.

What are the ten recollections? First, recollecting the Buddha’s immeasurable merits; second, recollecting the inconceivable liberation of the Dharma; third, recollecting the purity and freedom from defilement of the Sangha; fourth, recollecting the practice of great loving-kindness to establish all sentient beings in peace; fifth, recollecting the practice of great compassion to rescue them from all sufferings; sixth, recollecting those in the group of right determination and encouraging them to delight in cultivating goodness; seventh, recollecting those in the group of wrong determination and drawing them out to return to their original nature; eighth, recollecting the various hungry ghosts suffering from hunger, thirst, and feverish affliction; ninth, recollecting the various animals who constantly endure manifold sufferings; and tenth, recollecting the various beings in the hells who undergo all manner of burning and boiling.

The Bodhisattva reflects in this way upon the ten recollections: "I shall cultivate and accumulate the merits of the Triple Gem; I shall exhort myself toward loving-kindness, compassion, and right concentration; and I shall rescue and deliver those beings fixed in error from the sufferings of the three evil realms."

Reflecting in this way with focused mindfulness and without distraction, diligently practicing day and night without rest or cessation is called being able to give rise to right mindfulness and diligence.

Furthermore, there are four matters regarding a bodhisattva’s diligence, namely: practicing the path of the four right efforts (*samyakprahāṇa*)—preventing unarisen unwholesome states from arising, swiftly eliminating unwholesome states that have already arisen, employing skillful means to give rise to unarisen wholesome states, and cultivating, fulfilling, and expanding wholesome states that have already arisen.
When a bodhisattva thus cultivates the path of the four right efforts without ceasing, this is called diligence.
This diligent effort is able to destroy the realm of all afflictions and increase the primary cause for unsurpassed bodhi.
If a bodhisattva is able to undergo all manner of great physical and mental suffering for the sake of establishing all sentient beings in peace and does not become weary, this is called diligence.

Having distanced himself from the evil times of crookedness and perverse diligence, the Bodhisattva cultivates right diligence. This means cultivating faith, generosity, ethical discipline, patience, meditative concentration, wisdom, kindness, compassion, joy, and equanimity. With the desire to act, having acted, or about to act, he practices diligence with a sincere mind and without regret. Regarding all wholesome dharmas and the rescue of sentient beings from suffering, his mind never retreats or sinks, acting as if his head were on fire; this is called diligence.

Although a bodhisattva does not begrudge his own body or life, for the sake of uprooting all suffering and protecting the true Dharma, he ought to cherish them; he must not abandon dignified deportment and should constantly cultivate wholesome dharmas.

When practicing wholesome dharmas, the mind is free from indolence; when life or body are at risk, one does not abandon what is in accordance with the Dharma. This is called the bodhisattva’s diligent application of vigor while cultivating the path to enlightenment.

A person who is indolent cannot practice universal giving all at once; they cannot maintain the precepts, endure various sufferings, exert themselves with diligence, concentrate the mind in meditative absorption, or discern between good and evil.
Therefore it is said that the six pāramitās increase by means of diligence.
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva’s diligence is preeminent, they will be able to swiftly attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

When a bodhisattva arouses great adornment and exerts diligence, there are further four matters: first, the arousal of great adornment; second, the accumulation of valor and strength; third, the cultivation of all roots of goodness; and fourth, the teaching and transforming of sentient beings.
How does a bodhisattva don the great armor?

It is when the mind is able to endure all cycles of birth and death without calculating the number of kalpas; even throughout immeasurable, boundless hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas of *gaṅgā*-sands of *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas until the attainment of the Buddha-way, the mind never grows weary. This is called the diligence of tireless adornment.

A bodhisattva accumulates valor and exerts diligence; even if a trichiliocosm were filled with blazing fire, for the sake of seeing the Buddha, for the sake of hearing the Dharma, and for the sake of establishing sentient beings in wholesome dharmas, they would certainly pass through this fire.
To tame sentient beings, their minds are well-settled within great compassion; this is called courageous diligence.

When a bodhisattva cultivates roots of goodness and exerts diligence, dedicating all such roots of goodness toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* for the sake of accomplishing all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), this is called the diligence of cultivating roots of goodness.

A bodhisattva arouses diligence in order to transform sentient beings; yet the nature of sentient beings is incalculable, immeasurable, and boundless, equal to the realm of empty space. The bodhisattva makes a vow, "I shall deliver them all without exception," and practices diligence with the intent to transform and deliver them. This is called the diligence of transformation.
To speak in brief, the Bodhisattva cultivates the merits that assist the path to aid unsurpassed wisdom, and practices diligence to cultivate and accumulate the Buddha-dharmas.

The merits of all Buddhas are immeasurable and boundless; likewise, the diligence practiced by the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas who have resolved upon the Great Adornment is also immeasurable and boundless.
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices diligence with a mind free from desire in order to uproot the sufferings of sentient beings, they thereby fulfill the *vīrya-pāramitā*.
Chapter Eight: The Perfection of Dhyāna (*Dhyāna-pāramitā-varga*). From the *Bodhicittotpāda-śāstra*: How does a bodhisattva cultivate meditative concentration?
If meditative concentration is for the benefit of oneself, the benefit of others, or the benefit of both, such meditative concentration can adorn the path to enlightenment.
A bodhisattva practices meditative concentration because they wish to subdue sentient beings and cause them to be free from suffering and affliction.

One who cultivates meditative concentration skillfully restrains the mind, not allowing any distracted thoughts to intrude. Whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, one maintains mindfulness before oneself, observing in both forward and reverse order the skull, the crown of the head, the spine, the arms, elbows, chest, ribs, hips, thighs, shins, and ankles, while practicing *ānāpāna* (counting the breaths). This is called the Bodhisattva’s initial cultivation of the concentrated mind.
Because one cultivates meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*), one does not undergo various evils and the mind is constantly joyful; this is called self-benefit (*svārtha*).
To teach and transform sentient beings so that they cultivate right mindfulness (*samyak-smṛti*) is called benefiting others (*parārtha*).

By means of the pure samādhi cultivated by oneself, one distances oneself from evil thoughts and reflections, transforming all sentient beings so that they share in one's own benefit; this is called mutual benefit (*ubhayārtha*).
By virtue of cultivating meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*), one attains the eight liberations up to the *śūraṅgama-vajra-samādhi*; this is called adorning the path to bodhi.
Meditative concentration arises from three factors.
What are these three?

First, from the wisdom derived from hearing; second, from the wisdom derived from reflection; and third, from the wisdom derived from cultivation. From these three factors, all samādhis gradually arise.
What is the wisdom derived from hearing?
It is when one constantly delights in the Dharma as it has been heard and further reflects:
"The various Buddha-dharmas, such as the unhindered liberations, must be accomplished by means of extensive learning."

Having formed this thought, one becomes increasingly diligent whenever seeking the Dharma, constantly delighting in hearing the Dharma day and night without weariness; this is called the wisdom derived from hearing (śrutamayī-prajñā).
What is the wisdom of reflection?

It is the contemplation and observation of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) according to their true nature—that is to say, as impermanent, suffering, empty, non-self, and impure; as arising and ceasing moment by moment, and as soon to perish and decay.

Yet all sentient beings are bound by grief, sorrow, suffering, affliction, hatred, and attachment; they are merely incinerated by the fires of greed, anger, and delusion, thereby increasing the great mass of suffering and affliction in future lives, which possess no real nature and are like magical illusions.

Having seen this, one immediately gives rise to weary detachment toward all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) and applies oneself with even greater diligence to advance toward the wisdom of the Buddha. One contemplates that the wisdom of the Tathāgata is inconceivable and immeasurable, possessing great power such that none can surpass it; it leads to the great city of fearlessness and security from which there is no returning, and it is able to rescue immeasurable sentient beings from suffering and affliction.

To thus know and see the immeasurable wisdom of the Buddha and to see the immeasurable suffering and affliction of conditioned phenomena, while aspiring to seek the unsurpassed Mahāyāna—this is called "wisdom born of reflection" (cintāmayī-prajñā).
What is the cultivation of wisdom?
From the initial contemplation of the skeleton up to *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, all are termed the cultivation of wisdom.

Having abandoned unwholesome states associated with desire, and possessing directed thought (*vitarka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*), one enters the first dhyāna, which is born of seclusion and characterized by joy and bliss.

With the subsiding of directed thought and evaluation (*vitarka-vicāra*), with internal clarity and mental one-pointedness, free from directed thought and evaluation, born of concentration, he enters the second dhyāna, which is joy and happiness.

Through the fading away of joy, he dwells in equanimity; mindful and clearly aware, he experiences happiness with the body; he enters the third dhyāna, which the noble ones describe as "dwelling in equanimity, mindfulness, and happiness."

By abandoning both suffering and pleasure, and by the prior cessation of sorrow and joy, one enters the fourth dhyāna, which is neither painful nor pleasant, characterized by equanimity and purity of mindfulness.

Having transcended all perceptions of form, extinguished all perceptions of sensory resistance, and not attending to perceptions of diversity, one perceives infinite space and thus enters the sphere of the formless concentration of infinite space.
Transcending all characteristics of space, one knows infinite consciousness and thereby enters the formless meditative station of the base of infinite consciousness.
Transcending all characteristics of consciousness, one knows nothing exists and thereby enters the formless meditative station of the base of nothingness.
Transcending the sphere of nothingness, knowing the security of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, one enters the formless sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.

Because they practice in accordance with all phenomena without attachment, seeking the Unsurpassed Vehicle to achieve supreme perfect enlightenment, this is called the cultivation of wisdom (*bhāvanā-prajñā*).

When Bodhisattvas, based on this wisdom derived from hearing, reflection, and cultivation, diligently restrain the mind, they are then able to accomplish the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), the insights (*vidyā*), the samādhis, and the perfection of dhyāna (*dhyāna-pāramitā*).
Furthermore, there are ten further practices of the bodhisattva’s cultivation of concentration that are not shared with śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.
What are these ten?
First, the cultivation of concentration is free from the notion of self, because it is fully endowed with all the dhyānas and samādhis of the Tathāgata.
Second, one cultivates meditative concentration without relishing it or becoming attached to it, because one abandons defiled states of mind and does not seek personal pleasure.
Third, one cultivates meditative concentration to perfect the various supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), in order to know the mental activities of all sentient beings.
Fourth, one cultivates meditative concentration in order to know the minds of the multitude, for the sake of liberating all sentient beings.
Fifth, one cultivates meditative concentration to practice great compassion, for the sake of severing the fetters of affliction of all sentient beings.
Sixth, one cultivates meditative concentration through the various dhyānas and samādhis, because one skillfully knows how to enter and emerge from them, transcending the three realms.
Seventh, one cultivates meditative concentration to constantly attain mastery, because one is fully endowed with all wholesome dharmas.
Eighth, by cultivating meditative concentration, the mind attains quiescence, for it surpasses the various dhyānas and samādhis of the two vehicles.
Ninth, by cultivating meditative concentration, one constantly enters into wisdom, transcending all worldly realms to reach the other shore.
Tenth, by cultivating meditative concentration, one is able to promote the True Dharma and ensure that the Three Jewels are sustained and never severed.
Such concentration as this is not shared with śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.

Furthermore, in order to know the defiled minds of all sentient beings, one cultivates and accumulates the various dharmas of meditative concentration (dhyāna-samādhi) to assist in the stabilization of the mind; causing this meditative concentration to abide in an equanimous mind is what is called "concentration" (samādhi).
Samādhis such as these are equal to emptiness (*śūnyatā*), signlessness (*animitta*), wishlessness (*apraṇihita*), and non-action (*anabhisaṃskāra*).

That which is equal to emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, and non-action is equal to sentient beings; that which is equal to sentient beings is equal to all phenomena (*dharma*). To enter into such equality is called "samādhi."

Furthermore, although a bodhisattva acts in accordance with the world, he is not defiled by the world; he abandons the eight worldly dharmas, extinguishes all fetters, stays far removed from clamor and bustle, and delights in solitary dwelling.
When a bodhisattva practices meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) in this manner, the mind dwells in tranquility, detached from worldly activities.
Furthermore, the bodhisattva cultivates concentration because they possess the various supernormal knowledges (*abhijñā*), wisdom, skillful means (*upāya*), and insight (*prajñā*).
What are the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*)?
What is wisdom (*jñāna*)?

Whether it be seeing forms, hearing sounds, knowing the minds of others, recollecting the past, or being able to travel everywhere throughout the worlds of all Buddhas—these are called supernormal powers.

If one knows that form is itself the dharma-nature, understands that the nature and characteristics of sounds and mental activities are quiescent and equal throughout the three periods of time, and realizes that the realms of all Buddhas share the same characteristic as space without realizing cessation—this is called wisdom.
What is skillful means? What is wisdom?

When entering meditative concentration, giving rise to great compassion and not abandoning one’s vows, with a mind as firm as a diamond, observing the worlds of all Buddhas and adorning the site of enlightenment—this is called skillful means.

Their minds are eternally tranquil, devoid of self and sentient beings; they contemplate the fundamental nature of all phenomena without distraction, seeing the realms of all Buddhas as identical to empty space and observing their adornments as identical to quiescent extinction—this is called wisdom.

This is called the bodhisattva’s cultivation of meditative concentration; because it is distinguished by the integration of supernormal powers, wisdom, skillful means, and insight, these four matters are practiced together, enabling one to draw near to *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices meditative concentration (dhyāna) without any remaining unwholesome thoughts, by virtue of the quality of immovability, they thereby fulfill the dhyānapāramitā.
Chapter Nine: The Perfection of Wisdom (Prajñāpāramitā-varga) from the *Bodhicittotpāda-śāstra*. How does a bodhisattva cultivate wisdom?
If wisdom is for the benefit of oneself, the benefit of others, or the benefit of both, such wisdom can adorn the path to enlightenment.
A bodhisattva cultivates wisdom because they desire to subdue sentient beings and cause them to be free from suffering and affliction.

One who cultivates wisdom studies all worldly affairs, abandons greed, hatred, and delusion, and establishes a mind of loving-kindness; out of compassion, they benefit all sentient beings, constantly mindful of delivering them and acting as their guide. They are able to discern and explain the right path and the wrong path, as well as the retributions of good and evil. This is called the Bodhisattva’s initial mind of wisdom.
By cultivating wisdom, one distances oneself from ignorance and eliminates the hindrance of afflictions as well as the hindrance to wisdom; this is called self-benefit.
To transform sentient beings and cause them to attain subduing [of their defilements] is called benefiting others.
To transform all sentient beings through one's own cultivation of unsurpassed bodhi so that they attain benefits equal to one's own is called "mutual benefit.
By cultivating wisdom, one attains the first stage up to the knowledge of omniscience (*sarvajñā-jñāna*); this is called "adorned with the path to bodhi."
When a bodhisattva practices wisdom, there are twenty mental states that can gradually establish it.
What are these twenty? They are:
the mind of generating wholesome aspiration and drawing near to virtuous friends; the mind of abandoning arrogance and practicing heedfulness; the mind of following...

A mind that delights in hearing the Dharma by following the teachings; a mind of skillful reflection that never tires of hearing the Dharma; a mind that practices right knowledge by cultivating the four Brahma-vihāras;
a mind that gives rise to renunciation by contemplating impurity; a mind of the sixteen noble insights by contemplating the Four Noble Truths;
a mind that cultivates clear wisdom by contemplating the twelve links of dependent origination; and a mind that recollects all the pāramitās upon hearing them.

The mind that seeks to cultivate and accumulate; the mind that contemplates impermanence, suffering, non-self, and cessation; the mind that contemplates emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, and lack of effort;
the mind that contemplates the many faults and afflictions of the aggregates, elements, and sense bases; the mind that subdues the afflictions as one's adversaries;
the mind that protects all wholesome dharmas as one's own companions; and the mind that restrains unwholesome dharmas so they may be eliminated and severed.
The mind that cultivates the true Dharma so that it increases and expands; the mind that, though practicing the two vehicles, always remains detached from them;

the mind that, upon hearing the Bodhisattva-piṭaka, delights in its practice and observance; the mind that accords with and advances in all wholesome deeds for the sake of self-benefit and the benefit of others;
and the mind that maintains authentic conduct while seeking all Buddha-dharmas.
Furthermore, when a bodhisattva practices wisdom, there are ten further dharmas of skillful mental reflection that are not shared with śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.
What are these ten?

Contemplate and discern the roots of concentration and wisdom; contemplate and do not abandon the two extremes of eternalism and nihilism; contemplate that all phenomena arise through causes and conditions; contemplate that there is no sentient being, self, person, or life-span; contemplate that there are no phenomena of the three periods of time—past, future, or present; contemplate that while there is no deliberate effort, one does not sever the continuity of cause and effect; contemplate the emptiness of phenomena yet cultivate goodness without slackening; contemplate signlessness yet deliver sentient beings without ceasing; contemplate wishlessness yet seek bodhi without departing from it; and contemplate non-action yet manifest the reception of a body without forsaking it.
Furthermore, there are twelve gateways of skillful entry for a bodhisattva.
What are these twelve? They are:
skillfully entering the samādhis of emptiness and so forth without realizing [the ultimate fruit], and skillfully entering the various dhyāna-samādhis without following [their meditative states].
Skillfully entering the wisdom of the various supernormal powers born of dhyāna without realizing the untainted dharmas;

skillfully entering the method of internal contemplation without realizing fixed determination; skillfully entering the contemplation that all sentient beings are empty and quiescent without abandoning great loving-kindness;
skillfully entering the contemplation that all sentient beings are without self without abandoning great compassion; skillfully entering the generation of all...
Entering the miserable realms not by way of karma; entering the state of detachment from desire without yet realizing the dharma of detachment;
entering the relinquishing of the pleasure of desires without relinquishing the joy of the Dharma;

entering the relinquishing of all conceptual proliferation and discursive thoughts without relinquishing skillful means and various contemplations; and entering the reflection that conditioned phenomena possess many faults and afflictions—without...
Having relinquished the conditioned, they skillfully enter the purity and seclusion of unconditioned phenomena, yet they do not abide in the unconditioned.
When a bodhisattva is able to cultivate all dharmas of skillful entry, they are then able to skillfully understand that the three periods of time are empty and non-existent.

If one performs this contemplation, by the power of wisdom that contemplates the emptiness of the three periods of time, all immeasurable merits planted before the Buddhas of the three periods are entirely dedicated toward unexcelled bodhi; this is called the Bodhisattva’s skillful means of skillfully contemplating the three periods of time.
Furthermore, although one perceives that past phenomena, being subject to exhaustion, do not reach the future, one constantly cultivates goodness with diligent effort and without slackening;
although one observes that future phenomena have no arising or production, one does not abandon diligence and vows to advance toward Bodhi;

and although one observes that present phenomena perish moment by moment, the mind never forgets its resolve to set out for Bodhi—this is called the Bodhisattva’s skillful means of observing the three periods of time.

The past has already ceased, the future has not yet arrived, and the present does not abide; although one thus contemplates how the mind and mental factors arise, cease, disperse, and perish, one never abandons the accumulation of roots of goodness that assist the dharma of enlightenment—this is called the bodhisattva’s skillful means regarding the three periods of time.

Furthermore, the Bodhisattva contemplates all that is wholesome and unwholesome, self and non-self, real and unreal, empty and non-empty, conventional truth and ultimate truth, right determination and wrong determination, conditioned and unconditioned, out-flowing and non-out-flowing, dark dharmas and bright dharmas, birth-and-death and nirvana, as being of one mark and markless, like the nature of the dharma-realm. Within this, there is no dharma that can be named "markless," nor is there any dharma that serves as "markless. This is called the seal of all dharmas, the indestructible seal; within this seal, there is also no characteristic of a seal. This is called true wisdom, skillful means, and the Prajñāpāramitā.
A Bodhisattva Mahāsattva who has resolved upon bodhicitta should train in this way and practice in this way; one who practices in this way draws near to anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva practices wisdom with a mind that has no objective sphere of activity, because the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is pure, this constitutes the fulfillment of the *prajñāpāramitā*.

Chapter Ten: The Dharma-Gate of Reality (*Yathābhūta-dharmamukha*). In the *Bodhicittotpāda-śāstra*, Chapter Ten: The Dharma-Gate of Reality. If a son of good family or a daughter of good family cultivates the six *pāramitās* and seeks *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, they should abandon seven things.
What are the seven?
First, one should distance oneself from evil associates.
An evil associate is one who teaches others to abandon supreme faith, supreme aspiration, and supreme diligence, and instead to accumulate various miscellaneous practices.
Second, they distance themselves from female forms, from craving and indulgence in sensual desires, and from associating with worldly people while performing administrative duties.

Third, they distance themselves from evil thoughts, such as observing their own physical appearance with greed and attachment, cherishing it, and being stained by the desire to guard it, thinking it can be preserved for long.
Fourth, one should distance oneself from anger, violence, arrogance, jealousy, and envy, which give rise to disputes and ruin the virtuous mind.
Fifth, one should distance oneself from negligence, pride, and laziness, as well as the self-reliance on minor virtues that leads to the disparagement of others.

Sixth, one should distance oneself from the treatises of non-Buddhists, as well as from worldly prose and verse, flowery rhetoric, and anything not spoken by the Buddha that should not be praised or recited.
Seventh, one should not associate with those who hold wrong views or evil perspectives.
These seven dharmas are to be avoided.
The Tathāgata has said:
"I do not see any other dharma that more deeply obstructs the path to Buddhahood than these seven dharmas."
Therefore, a bodhisattva should remain far removed from them.
If one wishes to swiftly attain unsurpassed enlightenment, one should cultivate seven dharmas.
What are these seven?
First, a bodhisattva should draw near to spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*).

Spiritual friends are those who are the Buddhas and bodhisattvas, as well as śrāvakas, who are able to cause the bodhisattva to abide in the profound treasury of the Dharma and the various *pāramitās*; these, too, are the bodhisattva’s spiritual friends.

Second, a bodhisattva should associate with those who have left the household life and should also associate with the dharma of the araṇya; they should remain aloof from female forms and all sensual desires, and not engage in worldly affairs together with laypeople.

Third, a bodhisattva should observe themselves as follows: this body is like excrement and soil, containing nothing but foul odors and filth; it is subject to wind, cold, heat, and blood, and there is nothing in it to be greedily attached to. Since death must come one day, one should contemplate wearying detachment and diligently cultivate the Way.
Fourth, a bodhisattva should constantly practice harmony, patience, respect, and gentleness, and should also exhort and transform others to abide in patience.

Fifth, a bodhisattva should cultivate and accumulate diligence, constantly give rise to a sense of shame and remorse, reverently serve teachers and elders, have compassion for the poor and lowly, and when seeing those in distress and suffering, take their place with one's own body.
Sixth, a bodhisattva should cultivate the Vaipulya Mahāyāna Bodhisattva-piṭaka and uphold, recite, and study the dharmas praised by the Buddha.
Seventh, a bodhisattva should draw near to and cultivate the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya), namely, the true mark, the single mark, and the markless.
If bodhisattvas wish to swiftly attain unexcelled enlightenment, they should draw near to these seven dharmas.

Furthermore, if a person generates the mind of enlightenment but does so with the notion of attainment, and for immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas cultivates and accumulates loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity, as well as generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom—it should be known that such a person does not depart from birth and death, nor do they advance toward enlightenment.

Why is this? Because there is the mind that grasps at attainment and various views of attainment; views regarding the aggregates, elements, and sense bases; views of a self, a person, a sentient being, and a life span; and views regarding [the perfections of] loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity, as well as giving, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom.

To state the essentials: views regarding the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha, as well as views regarding nirvāṇa—such views that involve apprehension are attachments; mental attachment is what is called wrong view.

Why is this so? Those with false views revolve within the three realms and are forever separated from the essential means of liberation; those who harbor such attachments are likewise forever separated from the essential means of liberation and can ultimately never attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
If a person gives rise to the bodhicitta, they should contemplate the empty nature of this mind.
What is this mind?
What is its empty nature?
What is called "mind" is the mental consciousness; it is the aggregate of consciousness (vijñāna-skandha), the sense-base of mind (mana-āyatana), and the element of mind (mano-dhātu).
As for the empty characteristic of the mind, the mind lacks the characteristic of mind and likewise lacks an agent.
Why is this? Because the characteristics of this mind are empty; there is no agent, nor is there anyone who causes an agent.
If there is no agent, then there are no characteristics of action.

If a bodhisattva understands such dharmas as these, they will have no attachment toward any dharma. Because they are without attachment, they understand that there is no karmic retribution for good or evil. In practicing loving-kindness (*maitrī*), they realize there is no self; in practicing compassion (*karuṇā*), they realize there are no sentient beings; in practicing sympathetic joy (*muditā*), they realize there is no life-force (*jīva*); in practicing equanimity (*upekṣā*), they realize there is no person (*pudgala*). Although they practice giving, they do not perceive a gift; although they practice ethical discipline (*śīla*), they do not perceive a pure mind; although they practice patience (*kṣānti*), they do not perceive sentient beings; although they practice diligence (*vīrya*), they have no mind of desire-aversion; although they practice meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), they have no mind of eliminating evil; although they practice wisdom (*prajñā*), their mind has nothing upon which to act. Regarding all conditions, everything is wisdom, yet they do not cling to wisdom, do not grasp at wisdom, and do not perceive wisdom.

The practitioner thus cultivates wisdom, yet there is neither cultivation nor non-cultivation; for the sake of transforming sentient beings, they manifest the practice of the six perfections while remaining inwardly pure.

When a practitioner thus skillfully cultivates the mind, the fruit of merit from the roots of goodness planted in even a single moment of thought is immeasurable and boundless; it cannot be exhausted in hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, and they will naturally draw near to *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Chapter Eleven: Emptiness and Signlessness In the past, at one time, the Buddha was staying at the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove together with a great assembly of immeasurable numbers.
At that time, the World-Honored One extensively proclaimed the True Dharma and addressed the great assembly:
"The various dharmas spoken of by the Tathāgata—being without intrinsic nature, empty, and non-existent—are difficult for all the world to believe and understand."
Why is this? Form is neither bound nor liberated; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are neither bound nor liberated.
Form is signless and free from all signs; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are signless and free from all signs.
Form is without thought and free from all thoughts; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are without thought and free from all thoughts.
It is likewise for the eye and forms, the ear and sounds, the nose and odors, the tongue and tastes, the body and tangibles, and the mind and mental phenomena.

Without grasping and without abandoning, without defilement and without purity, without going and without coming, without facing toward and without turning away, without darkness and without light, without delusion and without wisdom; it is not this shore, not the other shore, and not the middle current—this is called "unbound."
Because it is without bondage, it is empty; emptiness is called signlessness, and signlessness is also empty—this is what is meant by emptiness.
Emptiness is called non-conceptualization, and non-conceptualization is also empty—this is what is meant by emptiness.
Empty thought is also empty; this is called emptiness.
Within emptiness there is neither good nor evil, and even the characteristic of emptiness does not exist; therefore it is called emptiness.

If a bodhisattva thus understands the nature of the aggregates (skandhas), elements (dhātus), and sense bases (āyatanas), they will not grasp or cling to them; this is called the patience regarding dharmas (dharmanidhyānakṣānti).
Because the bodhisattva practices patience in this way, they attain the patience of receiving the prediction [of enlightenment].
O Sons of the Buddha!
It is as if a bodhisattva were to write upon the void of space, transcribing all twelve divisions of the Tathāgata’s scriptures.
After immeasurable kalpas, the Buddha-dharma had already perished; those seeking the Dharma could neither see nor hear it, and sentient beings, being deluded, committed boundless evils.

Yet, there were people of pure wisdom from other regions who, out of compassion for sentient beings, sought the Buddha-dharma extensively. Arriving here, they saw characters in the air; as the inscriptions were clear and distinct, they immediately recognized them. They read, recited, accepted, and upheld them, practicing according to what was taught, explaining and analyzing them in detail to benefit sentient beings.
Can one conceive of this person who writes the word "emptiness" in the sky, yet is able to proclaim,
cultivate, and uphold it, guiding sentient beings to bring them away from their fetters?
"O Sons of the Buddha!
As the Tathāgata has declared, in past ages while seeking the path to bodhi, he encountered thirty-three billion, ninety-eight thousand Buddhas."

At that time, they were all universal monarchs (cakravartin rājā) who, with every kind of musical instrument and article of enjoyment, made offerings to the Buddhas and their assemblies of disciples; yet, because they acted with the notion of attainment, they did not receive the prediction of enlightenment (vyākaraṇa).
Thereafter, he again encountered eighty-four quintillion and ninety thousand pratyekabuddhas, whom he likewise served with the four requisites for as long as his life lasted.
Following this, he again encountered six million two hundred and one thousand two hundred and sixty-one buddhas.
At that time, they all became universal monarchs (*cakravartin*) and provided offerings of every kind of pleasure throughout their entire lives.

After those Buddhas passed into *parinirvāṇa*, they erected stupas made of the seven treasures to honor their relics. When subsequent Buddhas appeared in the world, they went forth to welcome them and entreated them to turn the wheel of the sublime Dharma, making such offerings to hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of Buddhas.

All these Tathāgatas expound the characteristics of all dharmas within the dharma of emptiness; because they still harbor the notion of attainment, they do not receive the prediction of enlightenment.

Thus it continues in succession until they encounter the appearance of the Buddha Dīpaṃkara; having seen the Buddha and heard the Dharma, they immediately attain the patient acceptance of the non-arising of all dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). Having attained this patience, they then receive their prediction.

The Tathāgata Dīpaṃkara taught the characteristics of all phenomena within the realm of emptiness, delivering and liberating immeasurable hundreds of thousands of sentient beings, yet there was nothing taught and no one delivered.

The Muni, the World-Honored One, has appeared in the world; within the dharma of emptiness, he speaks with words and letters, teaching, instructing, benefiting, and gladdening so that all may receive and practice them, yet there is nothing shown and no receiving or practicing.

One should know that the nature and characteristics of these dharmas are entirely empty: the scribe is empty, the one who recognizes them is empty, the one who speaks them is empty, and the one who understands them is empty; they have been empty from the beginning, will be empty in the future, and are empty in the present.

Yet, because these bodhisattvas have accumulated the power of skillful means through ten thousand virtues, they have attained unexcelled, complete, and perfect enlightenment through diligent and tireless effort until their merit was fully perfected; this is truly most difficult and inconceivable.

To speak of the characteristics of all phenomena within the realm of non-existence, and to speak of the attainment of phenomena within the state of non-attainment—such matters are the domain of the Buddhas; they can only be understood through immeasurable wisdom and cannot be known through mere intellectual deliberation.
Bodhisattvas who have newly resolved their minds sincerely revere and delight in Bodhi; because they trust the Buddha’s words, they are gradually able to enter [the path].
What is meant by "trust"?
It is to trust in the contemplation of the Four Noble Truths, thereby eliminating all afflictions, false views, fetters, and bonds, and attaining Arhatship.
By faithfully contemplating the twelve links of dependent origination, one eliminates ignorance and ceases the arising of all conditioned formations to attain the state of a Pratyekabuddha.
By faithfully practicing the four immeasurable minds and the six pāramitās, one attains anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
This is called the patience of faith (*śraddhā-kṣānti*).

Sentient beings, within beginningless birth and death, grasp at signs and cling to them, failing to see the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*). One should first observe that the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) of one's own body are merely conventional designations for a "sentient being"; therein, there is no self (*ātman*) and no sentient being.
Why is this? If there were a self, the self should possess sovereignty.
Yet all sentient beings are constantly afflicted by birth, old age, sickness, and death, and thus lack sovereignty; one should know, therefore, that there is no self.
The absence of self is the absence of an agent; where there is no agent, there is also no experiencer. The nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is pure, abiding as it truly is.
When one observes in this manner but has not yet reached the ultimate, it is called "conformity-patience" (*ānulomikī-kṣānti*).
Once the Bodhisattva has cultivated the patience of faith and compliance (*śraddhānulomikī-kṣānti*), before long he shall attain the supreme patience of the Dharma (*anuttaradharmakṣānti*).

Chapter Twelve: The Chapter on Sustaining Merit (*Guṇadhara-parivarta*) from the *Bodhicittotpāda-śāstra*. When a Bodhisattva is fully endowed with the cultivation of the signless mind (*animitta-citta*), his mind never dwells upon the performance of karma. This Bodhisattva acts intentionally while knowing the characteristics of all karmas: for the sake of cultivating roots of goodness and seeking enlightenment, he does not abandon the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*); for the sake of cultivating great compassion for all sentient beings, he does not dwell in the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*); for the sake of the true and wondrous wisdom of all Buddhas, he does not abandon birth and death (*saṃsāra*); and for the sake of delivering boundless sentient beings without exception, he does not dwell in nirvāṇa. This is called the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva’s profound mind seeking *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
O Sons of the Buddha!
If bodhisattvas accomplish ten dharmas, they shall never fall back or lose unsurpassed bodhi.
What are these ten?
First, the bodhisattva deeply resolves upon the unsurpassed mind of enlightenment and teaches and transforms sentient beings so that they also resolve their minds upon it.
Second, they always delight in seeing the Buddhas, offering what is most precious to them as gifts and making offerings to deeply plant roots of goodness.
Third, for the sake of seeking the Dharma, one should honor and make offerings to the Dharma teacher with a respectful mind, listening to the Dharma without weariness.

Fourth, if one sees that the community of bhikṣus has split into two factions, engaging in mutual disputes and accusations of faults, one should diligently seek skillful means to bring them back into harmony.

Fifth, if one sees that the land is dominated by evil and the Buddha-dharma is about to perish, one is able to read, recite, and explain even a single verse so that the Dharma is not interrupted, protecting the Dharma with single-minded devotion, regardless of body or life.
Sixth, seeing sentient beings terrified by suffering and affliction, he acts as their protector and bestows fearlessness upon them.
Seventh, he exerts diligent practice to seek such profound Mahāyāna sūtras and the various collections of the Bodhisattva-piṭaka.
Eighth, having attained this Dharma, they uphold, recite, and study it, practicing according to what is taught and abiding according to what is taught.
Ninth, while abiding in the Dharma themselves, they are also able to exhort and guide many sentient beings to enter into this Dharma.
Tenth, having entered into the Dharma, they are able to provide explanations for it, instructing, benefiting, gladdening, and awakening sentient beings.
When a bodhisattva accomplishes these ten dharmas, they shall never regress or fall away from unsurpassed enlightenment.
A bodhisattva should practice this sutra in this manner; such a sutra is inconceivable, for it is that which can give rise to the seeds of all great compassion.
This sutra can awaken and guide sentient beings bound by fetters, causing them to resolve their minds for enlightenment;
this sutra can serve as the generative cause for those directed toward Bodhi;
this sutra can accomplish all the unshakable practices of Bodhisattvas.
This sutra is protected and remembered by all Buddhas of the past, future, and present.

If there are good sons or good daughters who wish to diligently cultivate and accumulate unsurpassed bodhi, they should widely proclaim and disseminate such a sutra as this throughout Jambudvīpa so that it shall not be interrupted, enabling immeasurable and boundless sentient beings to hear this sutra.

If there are sons or daughters of good family who hear this sutra, all such persons shall attain a mass of fierce, sharp, and inconceivable great wisdom, as well as immeasurable fruits of merit and retribution.

Why is this so? Because this sutra can open the immeasurable, pure eye of wisdom; it can cause the lineage of the Buddhas to continue without interruption; it can rescue immeasurable sentient beings from suffering and affliction; it can illuminate all the darkness of ignorance and delusion; it can shatter the four Māras and all demonic activities; it can destroy all the heterodox views of external paths; it can extinguish the great fires of all afflictions; it can dissolve the various conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*) arising from causes and conditions; it can sever the six most grievous illnesses of stinginess, greed, breaking the precepts, anger, mental distraction, and folly; and it can eliminate the obstacles of karma, the obstacles of retribution, the obstacles of dharmas, the obstacles of afflictions, the obstacles of views, the obstacles of ignorance, the obstacles to knowledge, and the obstacles of habitual tendencies.
To state the essentials: this sutra can cause all unwholesome dharmas to be extinguished without remainder, and can cause all wholesome dharmas to blaze forth and increase.

If there are sons or daughters of good family who, having heard this sutra, feel joy, delight, and give rise to a sense of rare wonder, you should know that these persons have already made offerings to immeasurable Buddhas and have deeply planted roots of goodness.

Why is this so? Because this sutra is that which all Buddhas of the three periods of time have practiced; therefore, when a practitioner hears this sutra, they should rejoice and consider themselves to have obtained great and wholesome benefit.
If there are those who copy, read, or recite this sutra, you should know that the merit and reward obtained by such persons will be immeasurable and boundless. Why is this?

Because the objects of focus of this sutra are boundless; because it gives rise to immeasurable great vows; because it gathers in and sustains all sentient beings; and because it adorns the unsurpassed, supreme Bodhi—the merit and reward obtained is likewise without limit.

If one can understand its meaning and intent and practice accordingly as taught, even all the Buddhas, throughout incalculable eons (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*), could not exhaustively describe the karmic rewards of such merit with their inexhaustible wisdom.
Wherever a Dharma teacher preaches this sutra, it should be known that a stupa ought to be erected there. Why is this?
Because it is the place from which the true and correct Dharma has emerged.
In whatever land, city, town, village, temple, or monastery this sutra may reside, you should know that the Dharma-body itself is present therein.

If a person makes offerings of incense, flowers, music, or suspends silken banners and canopies, and praises it with songs and hymns, joining their palms in reverence, you should know that such a person has already succeeded to the lineage of the Buddhas; how much more so for those who fully receive and uphold this sutra! These people shall achieve the adornment of merit and wisdom, and in a future age they shall receive the prediction of enlightenment, destined to attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
